comment.value: The authors introduce a general method for maximizing likelihood when it is intractable to compute, in the simulation-based inference setting (when samples from any p_theta are obtainable), based on Fisher score matching (with linear parameterization). The paper is supported with both theory and experiments. After discussion, all authors voted for acceptance. The main strength is that the paper gives a new, very generally applicable method for a generally important problem and demonstrates its effectiveness. The discussion centered around answering reviewer requests for experiments (in the high-dimension setting and in comparison to neural network models) and hyperparameter tuning, both of which reviewers found were answered satisfactorily.

author_final_remarks.value:
We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers for their time and constructive feedback. The review process has been invaluable in helping us improve our work.

The discussion centered on two key areas, which we have addressed in detail.

* **Score Model Parameterization**: The choice of the linear score model was a critical design choice for robustness and speed. While the Fisher score matching (FSM) framework is readily able to accommodate more flexible models, our experimental results demonstrate that the NN model is constrained by additional computational costs and stability issues.

In our revised manuscript, we will include an NN model in all experiments to contrast its performance with the linear model and develop a more detailed discussion of the tradeoffs. We will also discuss a promising future research direction based on a hybrid "semi-amortized" approach that uses a pretrained NN encoder model with the linear FSM model.

* **Tuning of hyperparameter $\sigma$**: We clarified our data-driven strategy for tuning the hyperparameter $\sigma$, which is based on matching simulated data to observations, as is common in many intractable likelihood methods, and does not require ground-truth data. The optimal choice of $\sigma$ involves a bias-variance tradeoff, and is connected to the likelihood's curvature, which is unknown in the likelihood-free setting.

We will revise the manuscript to detail the calibration scheme fully, develop a more complete discussion of the optimal $\sigma$, and address its sensitivity in high dimensions.

Furthermore, our revision will incorporate discussions and experiments on the scalability of the FSM approach, as well as discussions on connections to Empirical Bayes, amortization, and all suggested improvements to notation and clarity. 

We briefly reiterate our core contributions here. Our manuscript introduces the Fisher score matching technique, a novel approach for direct Fisher score estimation of intractable likelihoods, providing a fast, robust, and lightweight framework for tackling maximum-likelihood estimation in the simulation-based inference setting, and shows that the FSM approach is a likelihood-free analogue of Gaussian smoothing, establishing the link between likelihood-free inference and zeroth-order optimization.

We hope that our rebuttal and planned revisions have fully addressed the reviewers' concerns and have substantially strengthened the manuscript. Thank you once again for your consideration.

Dear Reviewer e3CT:

We thank the reviewer for their positive feedback. We are particularly encouraged that the reviewer found our work to be novel and theoretically grounded.

> (Score Model Parameterization) “Have you tried more flexible (e.g., neural) score models?” and "Limited to linear score models; unclear if more expressive models would help."

The choice of score model parameterization is indeed a central design choice, and all 4 reviewers astutely raised this point. We provide a unified response to address these concerns.

Our initial research started with a neural network (NN) parameterization, but we ultimately opted for a linear model to align with our goal of developing a fast, robust, and lightweight MLE method. While we acknowledge that a NN model could potentially better capture the relationship of the Fisher score, this flexibility comes with significant computational costs in the form of an inner optimization loop and increased variance. In order to empirically validate this tradeoff, we implement the NN score model (2 layer MLP, using 10 steps of Adam per iteration) and extend the experiments in Section 7.1 and 7.3 of our manuscript. 

In Table 3, we can see that as the dimension increases, the NN score model starts to become unstable, however the linear FSM is more robust and scales relatively well. In Table 4, on a more complex problem despite the additional complexity of the NN model, we are not able to outperform the linear model, and this comes with the cost of increased variance.

Our empirical findings show that a straightforward NN model is not able to match a linear model, and it remains an interesting research direction about how best to incorporate a NN model in our framework. One promising extension, inspired by the reviewer's comments, is a hybrid approach that incorporates both a NN and linear model. During an offline pretraining phase, we use our FSM method to train the NN model over a wide range of simulated data. Then, during inference time, we can leverage the NN model as an encoder and use the linear FSM model on the encoded observations, allowing us to maintain the computational efficiency of the linear model during inference. We will include a further discussion of this extension, as well as our discussion on the trade-offs between a linear and NN score model in a future revision of our manuscript.


> “How sensitive is the method to the choice of $\sigma^2$ in high dimensions?”

From a theoretical perspective, we expect to find that the sensitivity of the smoothing hyperparameter $\sigma$ increases as the dimension increases. That is because, as discussed in Section 5.2 of our manuscript, the $\sigma$ governs a bias-variance tradeoff in the FSM estimator. Further, note that the dimension of the parameter space $d$ appears in the bias bound in Theorem 5.2. Hence, when the dimension increases, we expect the bias to increase, and hence $\sigma$ will necessarily need to be decreased in order to control the bias. However, this inflates the variance of the FSM estimator, making the calibration of $\sigma$ challenging in high-dimensional settings.

Despite the theoretical challenges, we did not find the tuning of $\sigma$ to be a practical issue, even for the relatively challenging, higher-dimensional Generator inversion task, with a parameter and data dimensions of $50$ and $256$ respectively. 

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We will incorporate this into our discussion of the calibration scheme for $\sigma$, and further investigate the sensitivity issues of $\sigma$ in high dimensions in a future revision of the manuscript.

> “Your estimator is based on a local posterior $p\left(\theta \mid x, \theta_t\right) \propto p(x \mid \theta) q\left(\theta \mid \theta_t\right)$ induced by the proposal — this resembles an empirical Bayes procedure where the prior adapts during optimization. Could you comment on this connection, and whether an EB perspective might offer additional insights or extensions?”

We thank the reviewer for the insightful remark! Indeed, our FSM procedure can be interpreted as a sequential form of EB. At each iteration, the proposal distribution $q(\theta \mid \theta_t)$ can be seen as a local prior, with the parameter iterate $\theta_t$, the mean of the proposal distribution, acting as a hyperparameter. Furthermore, the smoothed log-likelihood objective $\tilde{\ell}(\theta_t; x)$ as shown in Theorem 5.1 of our manuscript, is exactly the log marginal likelihood of the local model, that is used in EB

2. Using $\hat{\theta}_\sigma$, we draw simulated samples, and calculate the average Euclidean distance between the simulated samples and observations

summary.value: The paper introduces a novel method for likelihood-free MLE by estimating the Fisher score via local score matching around each parameter iterate. A linear surrogate model yields a closed-form estimator. The method is connected to Gaussian smoothing and outperforms alternative approaches in simulation efficiency.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**

- Novel, theoretically grounded estimator for likelihood-free Fisher score.
- Closed-form linear model enables fast and stable optimization.
- Strong empirical results across diverse SBI tasks.
- Clear connection to Gaussian smoothing.

**Weaknesses**
- $\theta_t$ and $\theta_j$ notation may confuse readers due to overlapping roles.
- Limited to linear score models; unclear if more expressive models would help.
- Not amortized; optimization must be redone per dataset.

questions.value:
- Have you tried more flexible (e.g., neural) score models?
- How sensitive is the method to the choice of $\sigma^2$ in high dimensions?
- Your estimator is based on a local posterior $p(\theta \mid x, \theta_t) \propto p(x \mid \theta) q(\theta \mid \theta_t)$ induced by the proposal — this resembles an empirical Bayes procedure where the prior adapts during optimization. Could you comment on this connection, and whether an EB perspective might offer additional insights or extensions?

value: NO or VERY MINOR ethics concerns only

final_justification.value:
**Paper:** *Direct Fisher Score Estimation for Likelihood Maximization*

---

1. **Flexible score models** – New experiments with a 2-layer MLP showed it matches linear FSM in low dimensions but becomes unstable and higher variance in high dimensions. Authors propose a hybrid NN + linear FSM “semi-amortized” extension.

2. **Sensitivity to $\sigma$** – Theory: bias–variance tradeoff worsens with higher $d$ (Theorem 5.2). Practice: no major tuning issues found, but calibration discussion will be expanded.

3. **Empirical Bayes link** – Proposal $q(\theta'|\theta_t)$ acts as local prior; smoothed log-likelihood equals local model’s log marginal likelihood. EB view to be added in revision.

4. **Notation** – Overlaps in $\theta$ will be clarified.

---

summary.value:
This paper tackles the problem of maximizing a log-likelihood $\log p(x|	heta)$, with data $x$ and parameters $	heta$, in the simulation-based inference setting, i.e., when $p(x|	heta)$ is intractable but model simulations can be obtained. The authors present an adaptation of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm, where the gradient $
abla_	heta \log p(x|	heta)$ is approximated via score matching at each iteration. To be more precise, given the current parameter value $	heta_t$, they consider a Gaussian prior $p(	heta|	heta_t)$ centered in $	heta_t$ (with arbitrary scalar variance $\sigma$ defined as a hyperparameter) and propose to approximate $
abla_{	heta=	heta_t} \log p(x|	heta)$ by the conditional expectation of $
abla_	heta \log p(x|	heta)$ over the posterior distribution $p(	heta|x, 	heta_t)\propto p(x|	heta)p(	heta|	heta_t)$ (which I denote here as the "Bayes estimator"). Interestingly, the L2 loss induced by this conditional expectation can be written into a simulation-free loss similar to Implicit Score Matching (ISM), coined Local Fisher Score Matching, but with the advantage of bypassing the need of computing divergence of the approximation function. In practice, they minimize this loss over the class of linear functions wrt x, which results in an explicit minimizer and avoids intensive use of computational budget at each gradient step.

On the theoretical side, they show that the Bayes estimator of $
abla_	heta \log p(x|	heta)$ can be easily interpreted as the score of a smoothed version of the original likelihood (namely, Gaussian smoothing which is widely used in zeroth-order optimization), and quantify the bias of this estimator with interpretable quantities. Interestingly, they demonstrate that the quality empirical estimator (i.e., the linear approximation of the Bayes estimator) is intimately induced by a trade-off on the scalar variance $\sigma$. Finally, they present numerical experiments where they compare their method with a KDE-based SGD approach, and evaluate the robustness of their algorithm with respect to the hyperparameter $\sigma$ and the dimension of the problem for various tasks where ground truth can be made available (cosmology, generator inversion..).

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**
- I find that the paper is very well written, I enjoyed very much the reading : the organization of the sections and the results is well chosen and easy to follow
- although the presented approach may be simple (combining Gaussian prior with linear parameterization), the resulting algorithm is well justified in theory and very efficient in practice (notably due to the lack of divergence computation in the ISM-like objective) : the overall idea is very nice and has been thought to handle reasonable computational budget, which is key for practical applications
- this paper present solid theoretical results (Theorems 5.1, 5.2, 5.3), which are interpretable and may help for applications
- the proposed algorithm demonstrates better robustness to increasing dimension than previous work

**Weaknesses** 
- in my opinion, the major weakness of this algorithm is the choice of the scalar parameter $\sigma$ for practical applications. As explained above, it plays the central role in the quality of the Bayes estimator (a low $\sigma$ would increase the variance, while a large $\sigma$ would increase the bias) and has to be carefully tuned. As far as I understand, this hyperparameter has been tuned in the presented numerical experiments based on access to ground truth (hence, by minimizing the prediction error wrt the optimal parameter). However, in practice, such tuning would seem impossible since both ground truth and likelihood function are not available... Furthermore, this hyperparameter is fixed from the beginning of the optimization procedure, which may not be optimal in practice.
- a second weakness (which is acknowledged by the authors) lies in the linear parameterization of the approximated gradient : the underlying assumption is that $x$ is distributed according to a Gaussian distribution given $\theta$, i.e., $p(x|\theta)\approx N(x; f(\theta), g(\theta))$, which may be too simple for real-world applications.

questions.value:
- In practice (i.e., without access to ground truth), what is the strategy to tune $\sigma$ ?
- Have you considered (i) taking a diagonal covariance matrix to model the Gaussian prior $p(\theta|\theta_t)$ and (ii) optimizing the covariance on-the-fly (i.e., making it depend on $\theta_t$) ?
- Have you considered a neural network parameterization of the Bayes estimator combined with a joint SGD procedure (i.e, taking some local SGD steps wrt the FSM loss (2) at each global gradient step) ? I have the feeling that it won't be too much costly, while dramatically increasing the expressivity of the model.

limitations.value: The authors acknowledge two limitations of their work : (i) the potential lack of expressivity from the linear parameterization and (ii) the careful tuning of the hyperparameter $\sigma$.

summary.value: The paper presents an approach to estimate maximum likelihood (MLE) estimator is a simulation-based inference setting i.e. where we do not have access to the underlying likelihood distribution but can generate samples from it. The authors approach this by learning Fisher score with a local score matching technique. When the score is parameterized as a linear model, the authors derive a close-form solution for it. The authors present theoretical discussion on convergence and other properties of the estimator, and present various empirical results.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The main text is well written and easy to follow. The approach is clearly motivated and presented, with discussion on convergence and other properties of the proposed estimator. 

Regarding weakness, see the questions section.

questions.value:
Major questions--

- While linear parameterization for score is convenient in that it gives a closed-form solution, I expect it can be severely constraining in some settings. Have the authors considered using a more flexible model for score and solve Eq. (3) numerically? Some discussion on this should be done in the paper. 
- Along above lines, it also seems that currently the authors fit a new score model (W) at every point, but can this be amortized? Similarly, will have a training dataset (as is generally done in SBI) help with more flexible score model? Again, some discussion on this will improve the paper.
- The authors discuss the impact of $\sigma_t$, but is there any guidance on how to choose it for a new problem? Along the same lines, do the authors consider varying/adapting $\sigma$ over iterations (e.g. depending on where they are in parameter space or as they get closer to MLE).
- How does the approach scale with dimensions, both parameter and data dimensions? If I understand correctly, the highest dimensions in current examples is 20. Again, some guidance along these lines is necessary for new applications. 

Minor points -- 
- I would recommend the authors include the algorithm-box in the main-text in the updated version (given the extra page). 
- Dimensionality of the parameters is not given in MNIST example
- Convergence of FSM is difficult to see in Fig. 3, right panel.

limitations.value: While the paper does discuss some limitations, I believe it can be expanded.

title.value: Direct Fisher Score Estimation for Likelihood Maximization

abstract.value: We study the problem of likelihood maximization when the likelihood function is intractable but model simulations are readily available. We propose a sequential, gradient-based optimization method that directly models the Fisher score based on a local score matching technique which uses simulations from a localized region around each parameter iterate. By employing a linear parameterization for the surrogate score model, our technique admits a closed-form, least-squares solution. This approach yields a fast, flexible, and efficient approximation to the Fisher score, effectively smoothing the likelihood objective and mitigating the challenges posed by complex likelihood landscapes. We provide theoretical guarantees for our score estimator, including bounds on the bias introduced by the smoothing. Empirical results on a range of synthetic and real-world problems demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to existing benchmarks.
